title: Google Cloud Posts 82% Revenue Surge as Kerala-Born CEO Thomas Kurian Cements AI Dominance
excerpt: Alphabet's cloud division generated $24.8 billion in Q2 2026, far exceeding analyst expectations of 63% growth, as enterprise demand for AI infrastructure accelerated under the leadership of Indian-American executive Thomas Kurian.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Google Cloud revenue surged 82% to $24.8 billion in Q2 2026, exceeding expectations.
  • Cloud operating income tripled to $8.8 billion, with margins expanding to 35.6%.
  • Alphabet raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast by $15 billion to $195–$205 billion.
  • Thomas Kurian transformed Google Cloud into a major AI infrastructure player since 2019.

Google Cloud Blows Past Expectations

Google Cloud delivered its strongest quarter ever on Wednesday, posting 82% revenue growth to $24.8 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected a 64% increase, while buy-side investors were eyeing at least 70% growth — a bar the division cleared comfortably.

https://x.com/Analyticsindiam/status/2080188890053501434

The blowout performance, reported as part of Alphabet's Q2 2026 earnings, marks a sharp acceleration from the 63% growth Google Cloud recorded in Q1 and reflects surging enterprise demand for AI infrastructure and services. Cloud operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion, with operating margins widening to 35.6% from 32.9% in the previous quarter.

"The quarter was highlighted by accelerating Cloud growth, expanding Cloud margins, and healthy backlog growth, underscoring accelerating enterprise demand for AI infrastructure and services."

— Justin Post, BofA Securities analyst

The cloud computing order backlog — representing signed deals not yet converted into revenue — jumped to $514 billion, up from $460 billion in Q1 and a staggering 375% increase year-over-year. Bank of America estimates that more than half of this backlog could convert into revenue over the next 24 months.

AI Demand Drives Historic Spending

The cloud triumph came alongside record capital spending that rattled investors. Alphabet reported $44.9 billion in Q2 capex, up 101% year-over-year, and raised its full-year 2026 forecast to $195–$205 billion from the previous $180–$190 billion range.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=T8VNQ4cPFFY

The higher spending tipped Alphabet into negative free cash flow territory for the first time in its history as a public company, burning $5.9 billion in the quarter. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said the company expected free cash flow to "remain under pressure" and signaled a "significant" increase in capex for 2027.

Overall, Alphabet delivered revenue of $119.8 billion, up 24% and ahead of the $117 billion consensus estimate. Operating income rose 30.4% to $40.8 billion. However, shares fell approximately 7% on Thursday as investors weighed the escalating spending against the strong revenue growth.

"When we used to talk about Cloud itself, very few, a very small percentage of overall workloads and enterprises had shifted to Cloud. Now think about what percentage of workloads should be really AI native and AI enabled. It again feels very, very early."

— Sundar Pichai, CEO, Alphabet

Gemini and the AI Model Race

Beyond cloud infrastructure, Alphabet disclosed that its Gemini AI assistant had reached 950 million monthly active users, with nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies using Gemini Enterprise. The Gemini API now processes 22 billion tokens per minute, up from 16 billion in Q1.

CEO Sundar Pichai addressed concerns about Google's competitive position in AI model development, acknowledging areas that need improvement — particularly in coding and agentic capabilities — while announcing that the company has begun training Gemini 4. Google also started recognizing revenue from direct sales of its TPU chips for the first time, competing with Nvidia's GPUs, though the bulk of TPU revenue from existing agreements is expected in 2027.

From Pampady to the Helm of Google Cloud

The cloud division's rise from perennial third-place finisher to AI growth leader is the defining achievement of Thomas Kurian's tenure. Born in 1966 in Pampady village, Kottayam district, Kerala, Kurian attended St Joseph's Boys' High School in Bangalore alongside his identical twin brother George — now CEO of data management company NetApp — before both earned admission to IIT Madras and subsequently Princeton University on partial scholarships.

After graduating summa cum laude in electrical engineering from Princeton and earning an MBA from Stanford, Kurian spent 22 years at Oracle, rising to president of product development. He joined Google Cloud as CEO in January 2019, at a time when the division was a distant third behind Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

Under Kurian's leadership, Google Cloud has been transformed through aggressive enterprise sales, strategic AI partnerships — including a landmark deal with Anthropic — and heavy investment in custom silicon. Cloud revenue now accounts for more than 20% of Alphabet's total revenue, up from roughly 7% when Kurian took over. His twin brother George's parallel rise to the helm of NetApp makes the Kurian brothers one of the most prominent pairs of Indian-origin CEOs in Silicon Valley history.

What Comes Next

The results position Google Cloud as the fastest-growing cloud platform among the three major hyperscalers, ahead of Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, which are expected to report 32% and 40% Q2 growth respectively. Microsoft and Amazon report earnings next week, and their results will reveal whether Google Cloud's AI-fueled acceleration is unique or reflective of broader industry momentum.

For Alphabet, the central question remains whether the massive infrastructure buildout will deliver returns commensurate with the investment. The company has committed to spending over $120 billion in the second half of 2026 alone, with 2027 projections from Deutsche Bank ranging as high as $340–$345 billion.

As Pichai put it on the earnings call: "If anything, over the past year, we've gotten more bullish on the opportunities ahead. In my conversations with many CEOs, many companies, they're all still barely scratching the early stages of what's possible here."
